title: Dense retrieval and bi-encoders (DPR)
summary: Dense retrieval encodes questions and passages into vectors and finds passages by vector similarity. The DPR paper uses a dual-encoder (a separate encoder for questions and passages) and scores with a dot product. Its abstract reports the dense retriever beating a strong Lucene-BM25 system by 9%-19% absolute on top-20 passage accuracy, on its own question answering datasets. The paper also calls dense and sparse retrieval complementary and says combining DPR with BM25 can help. This is a research method, not evidence of what Google or Bing use. Practitioner inference: dense matching may help when a query and a page share meaning but not words, so test it alongside exact-match search.
actions: Treat dense retrieval as an addition to keyword retrieval, not a replacement, when testing your own site search.
Test exact-match queries (codes, names) separately from natural-language queries.
Do not cite the DPR paper as proof of how Google ranks.

myths.correction: The DPR paper calls dense encoding complementary to sparse representations and reports that combining DPR with BM25 can improve results in some cases.

items.prompt: DPR in the Karpukhin et al. paper title stands for Dense ___ Retrieval. Which word fills the blank?
items.explanation: The paper is titled 'Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering'. The P is Passage.

items.prompt: The DPR paper learns its embeddings with which framework?
options: A. A simple dual-encoder setup
B. An inverted-index scorer
C. A knowledge-graph lookup
D. A cross-attention reranker only
items.explanation: Correct: the abstract says embeddings are learned from a small number of questions and passages by a simple dual-encoder framework. The other options are not what the abstract describes.

items.prompt: True or false: the DPR paper reports that its dense retriever outperforms a strong Lucene-BM25 system.
options: True
False
items.explanation: The abstract says exactly that, on top-20 passage retrieval accuracy by a margin of 9%-19% absolute. This is the paper's result on its own datasets, not a statement about web search.

items.prompt: Which statement about how DPR scores a question against a passage is correct?
options: A. Similarity is the count of words the two share
B. Similarity is the dot product of vectors
C. Similarity is the passage's BM25 score
D. Similarity is read from a knowledge graph
items.explanation: Correct: the paper defines similarity using the dot product of the question and passage vectors. Word overlap counting and BM25 are sparse, lexical approaches the paper compares against; a knowledge graph is not part of DPR.

items.prompt: True or false: the DPR paper describes dense retrieval as a replacement that makes sparse retrieval redundant.
options: True
False
items.explanation: The paper says the dense encoding is complementary to sparse representations by design and that combining DPR with BM25 can improve results in some cases.

items.prompt: Which statement is NOT supported by the DPR paper?
options: A. Google uses DPR to rank all of its web search results
B. Open-domain QA retrieval is usually done with TF-IDF or BM25
C. DPR improved top-20 accuracy over BM25 by 9%-19% absolute
D. Dense encoding complements sparse representations
items.explanation: Unsupported: a research paper describes a method for open-domain question answering; it cannot show what Google uses. The other statements are in the paper's text.

items.prompt: Hypothetical: on a test set, a BM25 baseline gets 60 percent top-20 accuracy. If a DPR-style retriever gained the paper's reported 9 to 19 points absolute, what range would it reach? Answer as low-high.
items.explanation: 60 + 9 = 69 and 60 + 19 = 79. The paper reports the gain on its own datasets, so this is arithmetic on a hypothetical baseline, not a prediction for any site.

items.prompt: Hypothetical audit note: 'The DPR paper shows dense retrievers beat BM25, so Google now ranks with dense retrieval and keyword work is dead.' What is the flaw?
options: A. DPR learns its embeddings with a dual-encoder
B. DPR scores passages with a dot product of vectors
C. A research paper cannot show what Google uses
D. BM25 was not used as a baseline in the paper
items.explanation: The flaw is the leap from a paper's method to Google's systems. The other options are wrong: DPR does use a dual-encoder, it does score with a dot product, and BM25 was the baseline. The paper also calls dense and sparse complementary.

items.prompt: Case file (hypothetical site: Harbor Docs help center). Symptom: after switching to dense-only semantic search, queries for exact product codes stopped finding the right page, though the old keyword search found them. Evidence: (1) the DPR paper says dense encoding is complementary to sparse representations by design; (2) it reports that combining DPR with BM25 improves results in some cases; (3) it notes retrieval is usually implemented with TF-IDF or BM25. Practitioner inference: code lookups reward exact term matching. What is the best next step?
options: A. Keep dense-only and retrain nothing
B. Delete the pages that fail
C. Drop the product codes from the pages
D. Combine dense retrieval with BM25
items.explanation: Best: the paper's evidence favours combining dense and BM25, and the failing queries are the type exact matching serves (inference). Keeping dense-only ignores the complementarity evidence. Deleting pages or removing codes damages the content to fit the tool.

items.prompt: Case file (hypothetical site: a university library search team). Symptom: the team wants to replace BM25 with a DPR-style dense retriever. Evidence: (1) the DPR paper reports its dense retriever beating a strong Lucene-BM25 system by 9%-19% absolute in top-20 passage retrieval accuracy, on its own datasets; (2) BEIR says BM25 is a robust baseline; (3) the team has so far tested only on the 30 queries it used to tune the model (hypothetical). What is the best next step?
options: A. Replace BM25 now, because the paper reports a 9%-19% gain
B. Compare both on held-out judged queries, keeping BM25 as the baseline
C. Remove the BM25 baseline so only dense results are reported
D. Tell stakeholders that Google already ranks with dense retrieval
items.explanation: Best: the paper's gain is a result on its own datasets, BEIR calls BM25 a robust baseline, and the tuning queries cannot show how the retriever behaves on new ones, so compare on held-out judged queries (the trade-off is time spent judging). Replacing BM25 now treats a paper's result as a prediction for this site. Dropping the baseline removes the comparison. No saved source says Google ranks with dense retrieval (unconfirmed).
